title: Bidirectional BFS in London: Meet-in-the-Middle ⚡
description: Watch Bidirectional BFS route across a real street-grid style map by launching two BFS searches—one from start, one from goal. When the frontiers meet, you reconstruct the path with far less exploration than standard BFS.
ig_caption:
Bidirectional BFS: Why Meeting in the Middle Cuts Search Space in Half — How launching two simultaneous searches doubles graph traversal speed ⚡

In a street-grid (Soho-style) graph, standard BFS expands outward until it *hits* the goal—often exploring tons of unnecessary nodes.

Bidirectional BFS flips the script:
1) Run BFS forward from the start.
2) Run BFS backward from the goal.
3) Keep expanding level-by-level.
4) The moment the two frontiers touch, you’ve found the shortest path (in an unweighted graph).

Why it’s faster (the “in half” intuition):
If the shortest path length is d and the branching factor is b, single-source BFS explores ~b^d. Bidirectional BFS splits depth into two searches of ~d/2 each, exploring about 2·b^(d/2) instead—dramatically fewer visited nodes.

Coding interview takeaway:
Use Bidirectional BFS when the graph is large and edges are unweighted (and you can traverse backward). Track visited sets from both sides, and stop immediately when a node appears in both visited maps/parents.

Debate question: When would you *avoid* Bidirectional BFS—small graphs, directed graphs, or memory constraints? 👇
